title: Recruiter switching between ATS and LinkedIn on Mac: fixes that cut copy-paste
metaTitle: Recruiter switching between ATS and LinkedIn on Mac: fixes
description: Stop retyping candidate details between your ATS and LinkedIn. Mac fixes that need no purchase, plus where Lazur helps with the copy-paste loop.
targetKeyword: recruiter switching between ATS and LinkedIn
secondaryKeywords: copy paste between ATS and LinkedIn
intro: If you switch between your ATS and LinkedIn all day, you probably retype the same candidate details more often than you think. This page explains what that switching costs, why it happens, and the fixes you can use on a Mac today without buying anything. It also says where Lazur helps and where it does not.
tldr: Recruiters switching between an ATS and LinkedIn often retype the same details. Surveys put the loss at seven or more hours a week for some workers.
Most of the loss comes from tools that do not share one record, not from careless typing.
Fix your paste habit, pick one source of truth for each field, and batch transfers before you buy any tool.
Lazur can point at fields, guide you through forms, dictate notes and draft text. It does not click or move data for you.

blocks.text: What copy-paste between an ATS and LinkedIn costs you

The cost is real, but the numbers need careful reading. Most public figures come from vendors that sell products in this space. Workday, working with The Harris Poll, surveyed 6,100 professionals in finance, HR, IT and operations. All of them were active AI users at organizations with 500 or more employees. Of those, 82% said they spend significant time copying and pasting between systems.

The same study says one in five employees, 20%, lose more than seven hours a week to copy-paste type work. For IT professionals the figure is one in four. Workday also says its sample was not random, and that its sentiment questions were answered mostly by director-level and above respondents. Read these numbers as a direction, not a measure of your team.

Workday UK reports a similar pattern. Its research, fielded in March 2026 with 2,400 UK professionals, found one in four UK workers spend seven or more hours a week copying information between applications. Parseur, a document-processing vendor, surveyed 500 U.S. professionals in July 2025. It reports more than nine hours a week moving data from emails, PDFs, spreadsheets and scans into other systems.

Parseur also puts a dollar figure on the problem, and its release disagrees with itself. The headline says more than $28,000 per employee per year. The body says an average of $28,500. The release does not explain how it calculated either number, so keep it out of any budget you present.

blocks.text: Where the errors come from

Time is only half the cost. Each hand-typed value can also be wrong. A 2019 study in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association followed 6,930 paired results across 60 outpatient clinics. Staff who re-entered glucose results by hand produced discrepancies in 260 entries, or 3.7%. The paper's conclusion gives 6,390 pairs instead, so its counts are not fully consistent.

A 2011 experiment by Barchard and Pace, read here through a Docsumo summary, found single-entry error at about 0.95% of values. When a second person checked the entries, the error fell to about 0.027%. The original paper was not checked for this page, so treat these as secondary figures, not settled facts.

Apply the rate to your own week. At 0.95%, about one value in every 100 goes wrong when someone types it once. Multiply that by the fields you retype each week and the mismatches add up. A wrong title or phone number in a candidate record can send a client the wrong profile. The study was not about recruiting, so use the rate to think, not to forecast.
Why you keep switching between your ATS and LinkedIn

Most recruiters work across three surfaces. The ATS holds the pipeline and the official record. LinkedIn holds the profile, the messages and the search. A spreadsheet or notes app often sits in the middle as a personal tracker. Each handoff means reading one screen and typing into another.

Asana, a work management vendor, says the average worker switches between 9 apps per day. It cites its Anatomy of Work Index. The page gives no year and no share of time spent switching, so use the 9 as a rough sense of scale, not a benchmark for recruiters.
Common triggers in a recruiting week

items: The ATS has no clean field for something you found on LinkedIn, such as a recent certification or a language.
Your tracker and the ATS both hold the same stage, so one gets updated and the other lags.
Outreach templates live in one tool and candidate notes live in another.
Interview feedback arrives by email and has to be copied back into the record.
Nobody agreed which system is the source of truth, so people keep two copies.

blocks.text: Fixes you can use today without buying anything
None of these fixes needs a new subscription. They work on any Mac with Chrome or Safari, and each takes minutes to set up. Start with the first one. Measure for a week before you add the next.

items: Paste as plain text. In Chrome or Safari, use ⌥⇧⌘V, which is Edit > Paste and Match Style. LinkedIn formatting then stays out of your ATS notes.
Pick one source of truth for each field. Write the rule at the top of your tracker, such as: stage lives in the ATS, notes live in the tracker.
Use one note template. Keep a fixed block with role, location, last contact and next step. You then copy one block instead of five separate fields.
Batch the transfers. Move candidates from LinkedIn into the ATS in one block, two times a day, instead of after every profile you open.
Move small items with Universal Clipboard. Copy a short line or an image on one device and paste it on the other. Check the requirements below first.
Dictate notes instead of typing them. Hold fn and speak. The text lands at the cursor, and you check it before you save.

blocks.text: Universal Clipboard has strict rules. Both devices need the same Apple Account. Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and Handoff must be on, and the devices must sit within 10 metres (30 feet) of each other. Apple says copied content stays on the clipboard only for a short time. For multiple files, Apple points to iCloud sync instead.
Shortcuts for the steps you repeat on a Mac

Shortcuts comes with macOS, so it costs nothing extra. Since macOS 26, Shortcuts supports personal automations. Apple lists triggers such as a time of day, a file added to a folder, an app opening or closing, and Focus changes. Apple's Mac guide also explains chaining actions, so text from one app can feed the next.

A simple use is a folder trigger. Save each exported candidate file to one folder, and a shortcut can handle it the same way every time. Another option is a weekday 8:00 AM automation that opens the links you check each morning. Test with a dummy file first. Check which actions your macOS version offers before you depend on a web form.
Zapier, and when a paid plan makes sense

Zapier connects apps with automated steps, which it calls Zaps. Its pricing page lists a free plan with 100 tasks a month and two-step Zaps only. The Professional plan starts at 750 tasks, at $19.99 a month billed annually or $29.99 billed monthly. Check zapier.com/pricing for current figures, since prices can change.

Before you pay, confirm that your ATS and LinkedIn appear in Zapier's app list, and check what each connection can do. This page does not claim that any specific integration exists. We found no independent study showing that Zapier or Shortcuts cuts copy-paste time. Run one Zap for two weeks and time it yourself.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. It points at things and guides you one click at a time. It drafts text and types it when you ask. It does not click buttons, edit files or operate your ATS or LinkedIn for you. It is not a plugin for either.

So Lazur will not move a candidate from LinkedIn into your ATS. It can help you find the field, explain an error on screen, and type a message you approve. These are the parts of the loop it can take off your hands:

items: Point: ask where the current title field is. Lazur circles it and adds a label on your screen.
Guide: ask how to attach a file on this form. Lazur gives one step, then waits for your click.
Explain: hold ⌥⌘ and ask what an error message means. The answer comes out loud.
Dictate: hold fn to dictate formatted notes at the cursor in any app.
Snippets and clipboard slots: keep your note template and outreach lines ready to insert.
Research: jobs run in Lazur's own Chrome tabs and return a summary and a report. Check each fact before you use it.

blocks.text: Dictation is the part most people use every day. It removes a lot of typing from note writing. Dictation is unlimited on both the Pro and Power plans. You still choose which field the text goes into.

The trial is 3 days on Pro, with no credit card. It starts when you first open the app. Pro costs $18 a month, or $15 a month billed annually, and includes 150 AI actions. Power costs $120 a month, or $96 a month billed annually, with 1,000 AI actions. Current terms are on the pricing page.
Candidate data and privacy rules to follow

Recruiting data is personal data. Candidate names, contact details and interview notes need care. Follow your employer's rules on candidate data before you paste anything into a new tool, including an AI assistant. Some companies allow AI on candidate screens, and some do not.

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. A screenshot of a candidate profile still leaves your Mac when you ask about it. If your employer bars that, do not ask Lazur about candidate screens.

The same rule applies in regulated work. Lawyers, nurses and accountants should follow their employer rules on client or patient data before they use any copy-paste fix or AI tool. Your employer's policy comes first, even when a fix looks harmless.
Mistakes people make with copy-paste fixes

items: Pasting first and cleaning later. Strip formatting at the moment of paste, or LinkedIn styling spreads into your notes.
Building a tracker nobody updates. A sheet with two status columns always lags behind one of them.
Automating before the fields agree. If the ATS and your sheet use different stage names, every automation files candidates in the wrong place.
Treating the clipboard as storage. Universal Clipboard holds copied content only briefly, so save important text in your tracker.
Skipping the check. Read back the fields that matter, such as name, title, company and contact, before you save.

blocks.text: How to measure whether a fix worked

Time one candidate record before you change anything. Count the minutes from opening the profile to saving the record, and count the fields you retype. Repeat the timing after a week with one change in place. A stopwatch on your iPhone or a plain note is enough. Change one thing at a time, or you will not know what helped.
What to do next

Start with the free changes this week. Pick one candidate record, time the transfer, then apply plain-text paste and one source of truth. If the loop still takes much of your day, look at tools with real integrations and compare their own pricing pages. For tracker setup, see [Google Sheets for recruiters](/for/recruiters/google-sheets). For inbox steps, see [Gmail for recruiters](/for/recruiters/gmail).

If you want Lazur for pointing, guiding and dictation, the [download page](/download) has the Mac app. The trial is 3 days and needs no card. Check the [pricing page](/pricing) before you decide which plan fits your week.

faq.question: What is the fastest way to stop copying between an ATS and LinkedIn?
faq.answer: Change your paste habit first. Use ⌥⇧⌘V in Chrome or Safari so formatting does not follow the text. Then pick one source of truth for each field. Both changes cost nothing and take minutes.

faq.question: Can Lazur move a candidate from LinkedIn into my ATS?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. It points at fields, guides you one click at a time, drafts text and dictates notes. You make each entry yourself.

faq.question: Does Universal Clipboard work between my iPhone and my Mac?
faq.answer: It can, if both devices use the same Apple Account, have Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and Handoff turned on, and sit within 10 metres (30 feet) of each other. Apple says it suits small text or copied images. For multiple files, use iCloud sync.

faq.question: How much weight should I give the 82% figure?
faq.answer: Treat it as a signal, not proof. It comes from Workday with The Harris Poll, which surveyed 6,100 AI-using professionals at organizations with 500 or more employees. Workday says its sample was not random.

faq.question: Can I use Shortcuts to fill in a web form?
faq.answer: Not reliably. Shortcuts can run on triggers, such as a file landing in a folder, and can pass text between apps. Check which actions your macOS version offers, and test on dummy data before you depend on a web flow.

faq.question: Does Zapier have a free plan for this kind of work?
faq.answer: Zapier's pricing page lists a free plan with 100 tasks a month and two-step Zaps only. Before you rely on it, confirm that your ATS and LinkedIn are supported and check what each connection can do.

faq.question: Is it safe to ask Lazur about candidate information?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer and are not stored. Follow your employer's candidate data rules first, and skip Lazur if they forbid it.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Lazur runs on macOS on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, but it is not available.

costs.title: Hours you do not get back
costs.text: Workday reports that one in five employees lose more than seven hours a week to copy-paste type work. Most of these figures come from vendors, so read them as a direction, not a measurement of your own team.

costs.title: Errors in the record
costs.text: A hand-typed value can be wrong. A 2019 clinical study found 3.7% discrepancies when staff re-entered results by hand. Recruiting work is different, but the risk of a wrong value in a record is the same kind.

costs.title: Attention lost between tabs
costs.text: Each switch between an ATS and LinkedIn costs a moment of focus. Asana says the average worker switches between 9 apps per day, although its page gives no year for that figure.

costs.title: Candidate trust
costs.text: A wrong title or phone number in a candidate record makes the process look careless. Once a candidate notices, you spend more time on the apology than you would have spent on the fix.

causes.title: Tools that do not share one record
causes.text: The ATS and LinkedIn hold different parts of the same candidate. Nothing moves a field from one to the other on its own. Workday names disconnected tools as a main source of copy-paste work, and that matches what most recruiters see every day.

causes.title: Two copies of the same status
causes.text: A tracker sheet and the ATS often both hold a stage. When one gets updated and the other does not, people copy the status across by hand, then forget which copy is right.

causes.title: Work about work
causes.text: Asana and Workday both describe work about work, which is the time spent moving information instead of using it. A recruiter who moves data between tools all day is doing work about work, even when the job itself is recruiting.

causes.title: No agreed source of truth
causes.text: When a team never agrees which system owns notes, contact details and stage, people keep several copies. Each copy then needs its own update, and each update invites a typo.

causes.title: Templates kept in the wrong place
causes.text: Outreach templates often live in an email tool, while notes live in the ATS and feedback lives in a chat app. Every time you need a template, you switch apps and copy the text back in.

fixes.title: Paste as plain text
fixes.text: In Chrome or Safari, use ⌥⇧⌘V, which is Edit > Paste and Match Style. This stops LinkedIn formatting from spreading into your ATS notes. It takes no setup and works on every paste you make.

fixes.title: Pick one source of truth per field
fixes.text: Decide which system owns each field, such as stage, notes and contact details. Write the rule at the top of your tracker so anyone who shares the pipeline can read it.

fixes.title: Use one note template
fixes.text: Keep a fixed block with role, location, last contact and next step. You then copy one block instead of five separate fields. Store it as a snippet in Lazur or as text in your notes app.

fixes.title: Batch the transfers
fixes.text: Move candidates from LinkedIn into the ATS in one block, two times a day. This cuts the number of switches without changing any tool. Pick two fixed times and keep them.

fixes.title: Move small items with Universal Clipboard
fixes.text: Copy a short line or an image on one Apple device and paste it on another. Both devices need the same Apple Account, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and Handoff, and must be within 10 metres (30 feet). Apple advises iCloud sync for multiple files.

fixes.title: Build a folder shortcut in Shortcuts
fixes.text: Shortcuts comes with macOS and can run a personal automation when a file lands in a folder. Test with a dummy file first. Check which actions your macOS version offers before you depend on a web form.

fixes.title: Test a Zap on the free plan first
fixes.text: Zapier's free plan lists 100 tasks a month and two-step Zaps only. Check whether your ATS and LinkedIn are supported before you build anything. Time one week of use before you pay for more tasks.

fixes.title: Dictate notes instead of typing them
fixes.text: Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. You still check the text and choose the field. Dictation is unlimited on both the Pro and Power plans.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Pick one source of truth
plan.text: Write down which system owns stage, notes and contact details. Put the rule at the top of your tracker and show it to anyone who shares the pipeline.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Change how you paste
plan.text: Use ⌥⇧⌘V in Chrome or Safari for every LinkedIn-to-ATS paste. Time one candidate record before and after, and write the minutes down.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Build a note template
plan.text: Make one block with role, location, last contact and next step. Save it as a snippet in Lazur or as text in your notes app, then use it for every candidate.

plan.label: Morning
plan.title: Batch the transfers
plan.text: Pick two fixed times a day to move candidates from LinkedIn into the ATS. Stop switching after every profile you open, and keep the two times for the whole week.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Try a folder shortcut
plan.text: Build one Shortcuts automation that triggers when a file lands in a folder. Test it with a dummy file before you rely on it for real candidate data.

plan.label: Day 6
plan.title: Check your data rules
plan.text: Confirm with your manager or IT which tools may hold candidate screens or files. Follow that rule before you keep using any AI or automation step.

plan.label: Day 7
plan.title: Re-time and decide
plan.text: Time the same candidate record again. Keep the changes that saved minutes and drop the ones that did not. Only then look at a paid tool.
